RIDEAU LAKES LAKE ASSOCIATION COMMITTEE (RLLAC)
Wednesday, June 24, 2026
The Rideau Lakes Lake Association Committee (RLLAC) Meeting was held Wednesday,
June 24th at 10:00 a.m. at the Portland Hall.
Roll call was taken and the following members were in attendance: Chair Mayor
Hoogenboom, Councillor, Sue Dunfield, Councillor Debbie Hutchings, Township staff Tom
Fehr, Manager of Development Services, and Amy Schur, Development Services Analyst.
Committee members from the following Lake Associations in attendance: Clark Johnston,
Bass Lake Property Owners Association; Hansen Downer, Big Rideau Lake Association;
Mary Rockburn, Birch Island Resident Property Owners Association; Tom Belton, Chaffey’s
and Area Lakes Association; Lynne Jeffries, Lower Beverley Lake Association; Buddy
Penniston, Opinicon East Cottagers’ Association; Steve Hebert, Opinicon Property Owners’
Community; Karl Fiander, Otter Lake Landowners Association; Ken Watson, Sand Lake
Estates, Steve Lauridsen, Troy Lake Ratepayers Association, John McDowell, Upper Rideau
Lake Association and Margie Manthey, Wolfe Lake Association.
Also in attendance: Councillor, Paula Banks, Councillor, Marcia Maxwell, Bob Thompson,
Upper Rideau Lake Association and Eric Lalonde, Rideau Valley Conservation Authority.
Members absent with prior notice included: Rhonda Birenbaum, Opinicon Property Owners’
Community and Susan Millar, Parks Canada.
EMERGENCY ADDITIONS TO THE AGENDA
Chair Hoogenboom asked if there were any emergency additions or amendments to the
agenda. None were heard.
ADOPTION OF AGENDA
Dr. David Philipp was invited to provide the update regarding Bass Spawning Sanctuaries
instead of Mr. McDowell & Mr. Downer. Due to a previous commitment item 6.2 was asked to
be moved to 6.1.
RECOMMENDATION #8-2026
Moved By: Tom Belton
Seconded By: Margie Manthey
To pass a Recommendation that;
This Committee adopt the Agenda, as amended
Moving 6.2 Bass Spawning Sanctuaries to 6.1 to allow Dr. David Philipp to provide the
update instead of Mr. McDowell & Mr. Downer.
Carried:
DECLARATION OF PECUNIARY INTEREST & GENERAL NATURE THEREOF
Chair Hoogenboom asked if anyone had a pecuniary interest and the general nature thereof,
regarding any items noted on the Agenda. None were heard.
June 24, 2026
Rideau Lakes Lake Association Committee Meeting
Pg. 2
ADOPTION OF MINUTES
Minutes of the Rideau Lakes Lake Association Committee Meeting held March 26, 2026 were
provided to the Committee.
RECOMMENDATION #9-2026
Moved By: Steve Lauridsen
Seconded By: Hansen Downer
To pass a Recommendation that;
This Committee approve the minutes of the Rideau Lakes Lake Association Committee
meeting held March 26, 2026 as submitted.
Carried:
GENERAL UPDATES
Bass Spawning Sanctuaries
Dr. David Philipp gave a verbal update on Bass Spawning Sanctuaries giving brief
background information regarding previous studies and research conducted as well as the
results from the Ministries on their recent proposed bass spawning sanctuaries. Dr. Philipp
explained their next steps and planned projects. The following card was distributed to the
Committee with QR code and website for education purposes about the project.
Committee held a discussion regarding: great support from RLLAC members, putting up
signage on individual lakes only during spawning, fishing being down all around the region,
more education needed for fishers, focus on community based ethical fishing, adding
sanctuary information on the individual lake association websites and newsletters, posting
QR code at Rideau Lakes boat launches, creating a media release with relevant story, doing
a podcast and getting information to bass fishing tournament organizers.
RECOMMENDATION #10-2026
Moved By: Hansen Downer
Seconded By: Steve Lauridsen
To pass a Recommendation that;
The Rideau Lakes Lake Association Committee acknowledges the presentation and update
from Dr. David Philipp Re: Bass Spawning Sanctuaries.
Carried:
June 24, 2026
Rideau Lakes Lake Association Committee Meeting
Pg. 3
Tourist Campground Licensing By-Law
Mr. Fehr, Manager of Development Services gave an update on the Tourist Campground
Licensing By-Law. A paper copy of his power point presentation to PACA on June 17th was
circulated to the Committee.
Committee held a discussion regarding: comparison of changes between versions, concerns
about density & water quality, by-law needs to be reasonable enforceable, Lower Beverley
Lake Park (LBLP) would also have to comply with all rules and regulations set out in this by-
law, campground need to provide baseline maps, no campground will be grandfathered, lots
of deficiencies at other campgrounds as well not just LBLP, enforcement is currently
complaint based, compliance timeline and flexibility.
Mr. McDowell had previously emailed in a proposed motion for the Committee to consider, as
follows:
RECOMMENDATION #11-2026
Moved By: John McDowell
Seconded By: Karl Fiander
To pass a Recommendation that;
WHEREAS Council engaged consultants to recommend elements of a draft Campground
Bylaw in 2023, and public meetings were held to collect views from a broad cross-section of
taxpayers including campground owners, and these recommendations became integral in the
2024 draft Campground Bylaw passed at 2nd reading, and furthermore that these provisions
provided a balance between protection of waterways and operational freedoms, and that staff
at the time advised Council that the By-law could be enforced without staff additions.
THEREFORE be it resolved that the Rideau Lakes Lake Association Committee recommend
to the Council of the Corporation of the Township of Rideau Lakes that the proposed
Campground Bylaw discussed by PACA on Wednesday June 17, be rejected by Council on
the grounds that the environmental protections recommended in the original draft version of
the bylaw have disappeared or have been significantly reduced, and that the 2024
Campground By-Law be reconsidered by Council for adoption at Third Reading.
Carried:
RECOMMENDATION #12-2026
Moved By: Ken Watson
Seconded By: Margie Manthey
To pass a Recommendation that;
The Rideau Lakes Lake Association Committee acknowledges the update from Tom Fehr,
Manager of Development Services Re: Tourist Camping Licensing By-Law.
Carried:

THE CORPORATION OF THE TOWNSHIP OF SCHREIBER
BYLAW 13-2019
BEING A BYLAW TO APPOINT AN INTEGRITY COMMISSIONER
WHEREAS the Municipal Act, S.O. 2001, Chapter 25, Section 223.3 (1), authorizes the
municipality to appoint an Integrity Commissioner who reports to Council and who is
responsible for performing in an independent manner the functions assigned by the
municipality with respect to,
(a) the application of the code of conduct for members of Council and the code of conduct
for members of local boards or of either of them;
(b) the application of any procedures, rules and policies of the municipality and local boards
governing the ethical behaviour of members of council and of local boards or of either of
them.
NOW THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED THAT THE COUNCIL OF THE CORPORATION
OF THE TOWNSHIP OF SCHREIBER ENACTS AS FOLLOWING:
1) That Expertise for Municipalities (E4m) shall be appointed and act as Integrity
Commissioner.
2) That this appointment shall be subject to the executed Letter of Engagement,
attached as Appendix “A” of this Bylaw.
3) This Bylaw shall come into force and effect upon enactment.
4) This Bylaw may be cited as “Township of Schreiber Integrity Commissioner Bylaw
13-2019”.
Read a first and second time this 26th day of March, 2019.
Read a third time and finally enacted, this 26th day of March, 2019.

Act, and many other Acts, for the purpose of providing good government with
respect to those matters; and
Whereas the Ontario Municipal Act, 2001, S.O. 2001, c. 25, Section 5.3, as
amended, states that a municipal power shall be exercised by By-law unless the
municipality is specifically authorized to do otherwise; and
Whereas, the water systems servicing the Lakefield Area and the Woodland
Acres Area may have difficulty meeting the daily demands for water during
certain periods of the year; and
Whereas; the Township of Smith-Ennismore-Lakefield passed By-law No. 2002-
68, being a By-law to regulate and restrict the use of water supplied to the users
of the Lakefield Area water system and the Woodland Acres Area water system
and now deems it advisable to repeal stated By-law;
Now Therefore, the Council of the Corporation of the Township of Smith-
Ennismore-Lakefield hereby enacts as follows:
1. That, in the Lakefield Area, from May 15th to September 15th of each year,
those premises with addresses ending with an even number be permitted to
water their lawns and gardens on calendar dates ending with an even number
between the hours of 7:00 a.m. and 9:00 a.m. and between the hours of 6:00
p.m. and 10:00 p.m.
2. That, in the Lakefield Area, from May 15th to September 15th of each year,
those premises with addresses ending with an odd number may be permitted
to water their lawns and gardens on calendar dates ending with an odd
number between the hours of 7:00 a.m. and 9:00 a.m. and between the hours
of 6:00 p.m. and 10:00 p.m.
3. That, in the Woodland Acres Area, from June 1st to August 31st of each year,
those premises with addresses ending with an even number be permitted to
water their lawns and gardens on calendar dates ending with an even number
between the hours of 7:00 a.m. and 10:00 p.m.
4. That, in the Woodland Acres Area, from June 1st to August 31st of each year,
those premises with addresses ending with an odd number may be permitted
to water their lawns and gardens on calendar dates ending with an odd
number between the hours of 7:00 a.m. and 10:00 p.m.
5. Notwithstanding Section 1, 2, 3, and 4 of this By-law, watering of newly
seeded or sodded lawns shall be permitted on any day between the hours of
7:00 a.m. and 9:00 a.m. and between the hours of 6:00 p.m. and 10:00 p.m.
with a hand held hose until such time as the seed or sod is established.
6. Notwithstanding Section 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 of this By-law, in the event of an
emergency situation, whereby normal water volumes and pressures are
jeopardized, or where extraordinary circumstances warrant, the Chief
Administrative Officer of the Township of Smith-Ennismore-Lakefield, or
his/her designate, in consultation with the system operator, shall be
authorized and directed to take whatever steps necessary to alleviate the
problem, which may include changes to the existing water restrictions and/or
a total ban on lawn and garden watering.
7. That no other high volume uses of water shall be permitted except under the
direction and control of the Township of Smith-Ennismore-Lakefield.
8. Violation of any of the provisions of this By-law shall constitute an offence.
9. A surcharge in the amount of $50.00 shall be imposed upon the account of
any customer that is found using water in violation of any of the provisions of
this By-law.
10. That each day on which any violation described in the By-law is continued
shall constitute a separate offence and the surcharge provided for under
Section 9 will apply once for each day that such violation occurs.
11. That this By-law applies to all customers of the water systems servicing the
Lakefield Area and the Woodland Acres Area.
12. That the Township of Smith-Ennismore-Lakefield By-law No. 2002-68 is
hereby repealed in its entirety.
13. That this By-law shall come in to full force and effect on the date of passing
thereof.
Read a first, second and third time and finally passed this 15th day of June A.D.,
2010.

MEETING TYPE: Regular Council Meeting
To: Council
From: Jackie Trenholm, Deputy Clerk
Date: April 16, 2025
Subject: 2026 Municipal Election Matters
Report No.: 2025-529
TITLE: 2026 Municipal Election Matters
RECOMMENDATION:
THAT Council authorizes the passing of By-law No. 25-25, Being a By-law Relating to 2026
Municipal Election Matters (language(s) to be used for election forms/notices/information; use
of alternative voting method; use of vote-counting equipment).
PURPOSE:
The purpose of this recommendation is to enable Council to make certain decisions respecting
the 2026 Municipal Election, including the use of the "telephone/internet" voting method.
BACKGROUND:
Several items must be addressed relative to the 2026 Municipal Election, including:
1. Use of Alternative Voting Methods
2. Advance Poll
3. Early Voting and/or Reduced Voting Hours
4. Use of vote-counting equipment
5. Language(s) in Notices/Forms/Information
6. Payment of rebate for campaign contributions
7. Ward(s) review/changes
8. Electronic filing of financial statements
9. Submitting a By-law or question to the electors (question on the ballot)
10. Appointment of Compliance Committee
DISCUSSION:
Item No. 1: Use of Alternative Voting Methods
The Municipality had been employing the vote-by-mail (VBM) voting method for several prior
general municipal elections (2003, 2006, 2010 and 2014). This alternative voting method has
been successful, having yielded higher voter turnout rates over traditional elections in each of
the last four general elections.
While this method has increased voter turnout, compared to the traditional in-person polls, the
participation rate has decreased over the last decade-and-a-half, as follows:
• Voter turnout 2003 – 60.61%
• Voter turnout 2006 – 57.72%
• Voter turnout 2010 – 56.86%
• Voter turnout 2014 – 55.95%
Given this gradual, but steady, decline in voter participation, staff recommended the use of the
telephone/internet voting method in the 2018 general election, the 2020 by-election and the
2022 general election. Voter turnout for those elections was as follows:
• 2018 General Election – 55.21%
• 2020 By-election – 32.48%
• 2022 General Election - 33.10%
Given the trend in municipal elections, across Ontario, of having fewer voters participate in
such elections, achieving a 55.21% voter turnout in 2018 was excellent, and placed Sioux
Lookout in among the highest of voter turnout results in Ontario. By-elections typically result in
lower number of voters. The 2020 By-election turnout was approximately 2.5% higher than the
last by-election in 2015. The 2022 voter turnout was lower than the 2018 general election.
When there isn’t a mayoral race, voter turnout is typically lower.
Vote-by-Mail versus Telephone/Internet Voting – An Analysis
Election Principles
Despite which voting method is selected, it is the responsibility of the Clerk/Returning Officer
to uphold the following election principles:
• The secrecy and confidentiality of the individual votes is paramount;
• The election must be fair and non-biased;
• The election must be accessible to all voters;
• The integrity of the process must be maintained throughout the election;
• There must be certainty that the results of the election reflect the votes cast; and
• All voters and candidates must be treated fairly and consistently.
Vote by Mail – Overview
Electors receive a voting kit in the mail. They mail in their signed declaration form along with
their secrecy envelope containing their marked ballot. The declaration form is scanned prior to
voting day; the secrecy ballot is kept in a secure ballot box until the close of election. On
Election Day, Staff open the ballot boxes containing the secrecy envelopes and review each
ballot to determine if the ballot is spoiled or rejected. Staff then feed the ballots through a vote
tabulating machine or count them manually. Once all of the ballots have been fed through the
vote tabulator (or counted manually), the tabulator totals the votes and provides a printable
receipt of the results to election officials, or the totals of votes cast and counted manually are
reported to the Returning Officer.
Advantages and Disadvantages: Vote-by-mail (VBM)
Advantages:
Signed declaration – provides security against voter fraud
Improved size and efficiency. Desk top tabulators are hooked up to a PC laptop and can
scan 40 ballots per minute and results are quick. They also store the image of each
ballot for recount/audit purposes.
Longer voting period
Disadvantages:
With VBM, staff are required to facilitate vote tabulation by feeding ballots into vote
tabulators, or physically/manually examining each ballot, and must make a determination
with respect to spoiled and rejected ballots
Staff resources and time - secrecy ballot envelopes cannot be opened until close of
voting. Ballots must then be organized, reviewed, scanned, counted and then eventually
destroyed.
If not using vote-counting equipment, manual vote-counting is extremely time consuming
– unofficial results in 2014 were not available until 2:00 a.m. (6 hours after close of
voting).
Opportunity for Spoiled ballots – vote does not count (e.g. elector included ballot with
signed declaration card; no signed declaration form or no declaration form included;
marking on the ballot that does not indicate choice or there is no marking on ballot)
Spoiled ballots – the voter has no way of knowing if their ballot was spoiled. There is no
confirmation process.
Potential to receive voter kits by unintended recipient which includes the ballot
Postal service – takes five days for voter to receive vote by mail kit; takes five days for
municipal office to receive marked ballot with secrecy envelope (total 5-10 days) by mail,
unless dropped off at municipal office
Costs – more expensive voting method due to need for more staff; manual count;
training of staff, etc.
Internet/Telephone Voting - Overview
Internet Voting – Electors receive a Voter Information Letter containing a Personal
Identification Number (PIN) in the mail. They log onto the election server on any computer,
vote by using their keyboard in response to a virtual ballot, the vote is stored on the election
software. The elector receives confirmation of their vote by way of a confirmation number or
printable receipt. At the close of Election Day, the internet software totals the votes received
and provides a printable receipt of the results to election officials.
Telephone Voting – Electors receive a Voter Information Letter containing a Personal
Identification Number (PIN) in the mail. They call a toll-free number from a touchtone phone;
vote by pressing buttons in response to a voice recording and the vote is stored by the
election software. The elector receives confirmation of their vote by way of a confirmation
number. At the close of Election Day, the telephone voting results are combined with the
internet voting results for one total result. A printable receipt of the results is made available to
election officials.
It is recommended that both internet and telephone options be provided to electors for the
2026 municipal election.
Advantages and Disadvantages of Internet/Telephone Voting
Advantages:
Less staff and administrative resources required and less expensive overall (except in
first year of implementation, due to public education costs)
No ballot errors/spoiled ballots because the software does not permit it. There are built in
reminders or safeguards to prevent accidental voting
Voter is provided with confirmation that their vote counted by issuance or confirmation of
a receipt
Elector participation is real time and results are immediate
Ballot destruction after election is electronically completed and verified
Voter has the opportunity to review selection and make changes prior to submitting vote
Lowered carbon footprint; environmentally sustainable due to less paper required
Recounts are instantaneous and inexpensive
Most accessible form of voting. Allows persons with disabilities the opportunity to
completely mark their ballot in private without the assistance of a designated friend or
election official, therefore providing greater dignity
Disadvantages:
Not everyone has access to a computer or is computer literate; however, telephone
voting would be the alternative to those who do not have internet access or low levels of
computer literacy
Security and viruses; voter authentication - however, the preferred vendor has
implemented robust measures to mitigate such threats
Telephone voting takes time – audio ballot
Telephone voting - Voter cannot see the names of the candidates
Other Benefits of Internet/telephone Voting
• provides convenience, accommodates changing lifestyles, demanding work schedules;
• enhances accessibility for students studying away from home, those travelling, shift
workers, infirmed persons, and persons with language barriers.
• for persons with disabilities, it provides greater dignity and privacy for electors;
• engages a wider range of age demographics, provides greater accuracy and fast results, is
convenient for seasonal residents, and has the potential for increased voter turnout.
Public Education & Outreach
Public education and outreach will play a critical role in the 2026 municipal election, should the
telephone/internet voting method be adopted. Although this method has been used several
times in Sioux Lookout, to ensure that concerns and questions regarding this voting method
are adequately addressed, a prior election education campaigns will be enhanced and
administered by the Clerk.
In order to mitigate concerns regarding accessibility for senior citizens to vote, the Clerk, as in
the 2018, 2020 and 2022 elections, will arrange to attend multi-residential senior complexes
throughout the community to provide senior citizens the opportunity to vote at their residence.
Additionally, for those who are not comfortable with internet voting or telephone voting on their
own, an electronic voting station will be established at the Municipal Office, with staff on hand
to provide assistance, as requested. Furthermore, remote voting locations will be established
at the Sioux Lookout Senior’s Centre, the Sioux Lookout Meno Ya Win Health Centre, the
William George Extended Care Unit, the Nishnawbe-Gamik Friendship Centre, and in Hudson.
Accessibility for Persons with Disabilities
Internet/Telephone voting offers the most accessible form of voting. Voters are offered the
greatest secrecy and less assisted voting thereby enhancing the quality of the vote and
anonymity.
Security
Section 89 of the Municipal Elections Act provides for penalties for any contravention of the
Act, as follows:
A person is guilty of an offence if he or she,
(a) votes without being entitled to do so;
(b) votes more times than this Act allows;
(c) votes in a voting place in which he or she is not entitled to vote;
(d) induces or procures a person to vote when that person is not entitled to do so;
(e) having appointed a voting proxy that remains in force, votes otherwise than by the proxy;
(f) having been appointed a voting proxy, votes under the authority of the proxy when the
elector has cancelled the proxy, is no longer entitled to vote or has died;
(g) before or during an election, publishes a false statement of a candidate’s withdrawal;
(h) furnishes false or misleading information to a person whom this Act authorizes to obtain
information;
(i) without authority, supplies a ballot to anyone;
(j) delivers to the deputy returning officer to be placed in a ballot box a paper other than the
ballot the deputy returning officer gave him or her;
(k) takes a ballot away from the voting place;
(l) at an election, takes, opens or otherwise deals with a ballot, a ballot box, or a book or
package of ballots without having authority to do so;
(m) attempts to do something described in clauses (a) to (l)
Clearly, accountability of voting rests with the voter and there are penalties associated with
voter fraud. Unsupervised voting facilitates the potentiality of these offences. Voter
impersonation, coercion and fraud are concerns which are mitigated through the design of any
voting system, regardless of whether it is a supervised or unsupervised model.
Item No. 2: Advance Poll
The use of the vote-by-mail or telephone/internet voting methods eliminates the need for
advance polls. Additionally, determination of this matter has now been delegated to the Clerk,
via the Municipal Elections Act, Council no longer makes these decisions.
Item No. 3: Early Voting and/or Reduced Voting Hours
The vote-by-mail voting or telephone/internet voting methods eliminates the need for these
measures. Additionally, determination of this matter has now been delegated to the Clerk, via
the Municipal Elections Act, Council no longer makes these decisions.
Item No. 4: Use of Vote-Counting Equipment
The Municipality had used Electronic Vote Tabulators (EVTs) in the 2000, 2003, 2006 and
2010 Municipal Elections. Ballots were created and coded by Ward, School Board
candidate(s) and Municipal Council (Mayor and Councillors-at-Large) candidates and
processed by the EVT on voting day. In the past, this has resulted in election results within
minutes of the close of polls.
For the 2014 Municipal Election, the Clerk chose to use manual vote-counting procedures
given that vote-counting equipment rental had significantly increased in cost increase since
the 2010 Municipal Election. The primary impact on the election was a longer time-frame
between the close of polls and the announcement of the unofficial results – a total of six hours.
If Council chooses to use the Vote-by-Mail voting method in 2026, vote tabulators will be
required to ensure the efficient tabulation of results; this is an additional cost to using this
voting method.
Item No. 5: Language(s) in Notices/Forms/Information
Prescribed forms (those set by legislation) must be provided in English only, but may be
provided in English and French only. Other forms/notices/information can be provided in
English, French or any other language, providing Council passes a by-law permitting such.
In one previous election, prior to 2003, some of the Notices were provided in both English and
Oji-Cree. This exercise was costly and was subsequently discontinued. It should be noted that
the onus is on the elector to provide translation services when voting. In 2003, 2006 and 2010,
the Clerk recommended and Council passed a By-law to provide notices in Oji-Cree at the
discretion of the Clerk.
Staff recommends that Council permit notices to be published in Oji-Cree for the 2026
Municipal Election, at the discretion of the Clerk.

Recommendation:
That Council approves $5,000 to be drawn from the Municipal Accommodation Tax
Reserve, Account 34012 for the purpose of a Thursday night concert series at the Bluewater
Park Bandshell for the month of August;
And further that if sponsors are confirmed for the concert series, sponsorship funds will be
allocated to the Municipal Accommodation Tax Reserve.
Link to Strategic Planning: Goal 4: Healthy, Vibrant and Safe Communities
4.1 Enhance facilities for healthy living and affordable and cultural opportunities.
Background:
As part of a successful grant application through the Federal Economic Development
Agency of Southern Ontario's Community Revitalization stream, the Town of South Bruce
Peninsula was awarded $375,000. These funds are designated for upgrades to Bluewater
Park, including improvements to the pier and causeway, accessibility enhancements, the
bandshell, and indigenous and marine interpretive signage.
The bandshell construction is now complete, and on July 11, 2024, the Town hosted a
grand opening event at Bluewater Park. Local musicians Midnight Blue performed at the
concert, and the event was a resounding success, attracting over 400 attendees to the
ribbon-cutting ceremony and the concert.
The long-term goal for the bandshell is to encourage rentals for regular concerts and events,
thereby attracting visitors and creating a positive economic impact on the local economy.
The rental rate for the bandshell is set at $150 for not-for-profit events and $450 for for-profit
events.
In collaboration with a local musician, staff have organized a concert series featuring various
artists on Thursday evenings from 7:30 pm to 9:00 pm during the month of August, with
performances scheduled for the 8th, 15th, 22nd, and 29th. This concert series aims to
showcase the new venue and generate interest in future rentals.
With the summer season well underway, staff have worked expeditiously to organize this
series in advance of the first concert date on August 8th. For future Town-run events, staff
will seek sponsorship to support these initiatives.
Staff are recommending that the total project budget of $5,000 to fund this concert series be
drawn from the Municipal Accommodation Tax working capital reserve as these events
support a tourism attraction in South Bruce Peninsula.

Report To: Council, August 6, 2024
Report No: AD16-2024
Subject: August Concert Series Bluewater Park
Recommendation:
That Council approves $5,000 to be drawn from the Municipal Accommodation Tax
Reserve, Account 34012 for the purpose of a Thursday night concert series at the Bluewater
Park Bandshell for the month of August;
And further that if sponsors are confirmed for the concert series, sponsorship funds will be
allocated to the Municipal Accommodation Tax Reserve.
Link to Strategic Planning: Goal 4: Healthy, Vibrant and Safe Communities
4.1 Enhance facilities for healthy living and affordable and cultural opportunities.
Background:
As part of a successful grant application through the Federal Economic Development
Agency of Southern Ontario's Community Revitalization stream, the Town of South Bruce
Peninsula was awarded $375,000. These funds are designated for upgrades to Bluewater
Park, including improvements to the pier and causeway, accessibility enhancements, the
bandshell, and indigenous and marine interpretive signage.
The bandshell construction is now complete, and on July 11, 2024, the Town hosted a
grand opening event at Bluewater Park. Local musicians Midnight Blue performed at the
concert, and the event was a resounding success, attracting over 400 attendees to the
ribbon-cutting ceremony and the concert.
The long-term goal for the bandshell is to encourage rentals for regular concerts and events,
thereby attracting visitors and creating a positive economic impact on the local economy.
The rental rate for the bandshell is set at $150 for not-for-profit events and $450 for for-profit
events.
In collaboration with a local musician, staff have organized a concert series featuring various
artists on Thursday evenings from 7:30 pm to 9:00 pm during the month of August, with
performances scheduled for the 8th, 15th, 22nd, and 29th. This concert series aims to
showcase the new venue and generate interest in future rentals.
With the summer season well underway, staff have worked expeditiously to organize this
series in advance of the first concert date on August 8th. For future Town-run events, staff
will seek sponsorship to support these initiatives.
Staff are recommending that the total project budget of $5,000 to fund this concert series be
drawn from the Municipal Accommodation Tax working capital reserve as these events
support a tourism attraction in South Bruce Peninsula.
Staff are also seeking sponsorship for the Thursday night music series and if successful, the
initiative will be partially/fully funded via sponsorship. At the Time of writing this report,
sponsorship funding has not been secured, hence the request to utilize MAT funds. Any
sponsorship funding will be utilized to pay for the concert series and replenish MAT
reserves, if funding comes at a later date.
Options:
A $5,000 to be allocated from the Municipal Accommodation Tax Reserve for the
Thursday night concert series at the Bluewater Park Bandshell in the month of
August.
B. Provide alternate direction.
Attachments:
None
Inter-Departmental Impact:
The Manager of Economic Development will work with the Recreation and Parks
Department on venue booking and equipment set up. Communications of the concert series
will be through the website and social media channels.
(E
Financial Implications: Approval of Director of Financial Services/Treasurer
The funding for this series would be a maximum project budget of $5,000 or $1,250 per
concert. The Town maintains a Municipal Accommodation Tax Reserve, Account
34012, the funds of which can be utilized as determined by Council. The uncommitted
balance of the Reserve is $70,935.
Expected Date of Completion:
The concert series would be held every Thursday for the month of August, being on the 8th ,
15th , and 22nd with the final concert in the series being on 29th of 2024.

Council Meetings
Regular Council Meetings typically occur on the 2nd and 4th Wednesday of each month, with exceptions made during holidays. In the months of July, August, and December, Regular Council Meetings are held only once per month. Regular Council Meetings are open to the public and live streamed to YouTube.

Committee of Council Meetings
Committees of Council meet as directed in each committees terms of reference. Meetings and agendas can be found using the calendar below. Additionally, visit the Committees of Council webpage for information such as mandates, members, minutes and more! 
Types of Meetings
Meetings Open to the Public: Almost all regular Council and Committee meetings are Open to the Public.  The public is welcome to attend and observe.  These meetings follow a set agenda with all information being presented or discussed published in advance. There isn't a formal opportunity for observers to speak to Council or Committee members during these meetings.  If you have thoughts or concerns about a topic on the agenda, let staff, Council or Committee members know them before the meeting takes place. 
 Public Meetings: A Public Meeting is a special meeting where members of the public can attend and speak directly to Council or a Committee as part of the agenda. Comments from the public are formally documented as part of the meeting record. In some cases (like zoning changes), a public meeting is legally required under the Planning Act.  Council can also hold a Public Meeting when they want direct input on other issues.Come prepared to share your thoughts when you attend a Public Meeting!  
 Open House: An Open House is informal by design. The public is welcome to attend, ask questions and share feedback. There is no agenda or formal record.  An Open House is the chance to have a one-on-one conversation with the people working on the issue.

Welcome
Welcome to the Township of Springwater’s Meeting Portal. We pride ourselves on being accountable, transparent and accessible as possible. Through this Portal, you will be able to view agendas reports and minutes, subscribe to updates, search documents and more!
  Meeting transparency and participation
Be advised that meetings of Council are held as hybrid meetings, allowing for in person and remote participation that are open to the public. Hybrid meetings allow members of Council, staff, delegates and the public to participate in person from Council Chambers or a remote location.  Meetings will be live streamed at www.springwater.ca/live and will be available on the Township of Springwater’s  YouTube Channel . Questions about the live stream or meetings should be directed to clerks@springwater.ca
  New Question Period Procedures: In an effort to accommodate question period, the following process will be followed until further notice. Those wishing to submit a question or comment for question period shall have 2 options:
 1) Submit questions in writing. The Clerk will read the submissions during the Question Period portion of the agenda:
 a) Email clerks@springwater.ca with the subject line reading "Question Period Submission".
 b) Provide your full name, address and stated question or comment noting the accompanying agenda item number, if applicable.
 2) Submit a request to make oral submission. Members of the public may request to make an oral submission, in person or via electronic attendance through zoom, during the Question Period portion of the agenda.
 a) Email clerks@springwater.ca with the subject line reading "Question Period Submission".
 b) Provide your full name, address and stated question or comment noting the accompanying agenda item number, if applicable. Also note in the email that you would like to pose your question/comment as an oral submission, in person or virtually during Question Period.
 c) Once received, you will receive an email with further instructions on how to attend the meeting in person or virtually.
Questions and comments will be accepted once the agenda is published on the Township's CivicWeb portal. Submissions received prior to the agendas' release will not be accepted.
In order to accommodate the registration process for oral presentations, submissions will be accepted until 12:00 p.m. on the day of the meeting.
In accordance with the Procedural By-law, the first 5 submissions will be accepted in the order that they are received, on a first come first served basis with a total of 10 minutes to be dedicated to question period. Written submissions which are similar in nature may be dealt with as one question.
  Closed Session: Meetings may proceed into closed session (Private) at which time the stream will cease/stop, however once the meeting rises, the stream will reconvene. Depending on your browser settings, you may have to refresh your browser.

Welcome
Welcome to the Township of Tay's Meeting Portal. We pride ourselves on being accountable, transparent, and accessible. Through this Portal, you will be able to view agendas, reports, minutes, and by-laws, subscribe to updates, and search documents.
 Meeting Transparency 
Please be advised that all regular and special meetings of Council are held in-person in Council Chambers at the Municipal Building located at 450 Park Street, Victoria Harbour, while all Committee of the Whole meetings are held virtually. All Council and Committee of the Whole meetings are live streamed and will be available on the Tay Township YouTube Channel. Questions about the live stream or meetings should be directed to clerk@tay.ca.
 Strong Mayor Powers
Effective May 1, 2025, the Mayor of Tay Township has Strong Mayor Powers. The Mayor is required to exercise these powers in writing, give notice to the Municipal Clerk, and make decisions and directives available to the public, subject to the Municipal Freedom of Information and Protection of Privacy Act.  Mayoral decisions and directives are available on the Township’s webpage: Strong Mayor Powers
 Delegation Requests
Interested in providing a delegation to Council? Please fill out the Delegation Request Form and submit to the Municipal Clerk at clerk@tay.ca or in-person at the Municipal Building. Approved delegations will be allowed ten (10) minutes to present in front of Council or Committee of the Whole, with additional time provided for questions by members of Council. Delegations will not be scheduled if the matter has already been before Council and a decision has been rendered. Further, multiple or repeat delegations on the same matter will not be scheduled unless new information on the matter is provided. Please Note: information provided on the Delegation Request Form will become part of the public record and be added to the public Council meeting Agenda.

City Council meets regularly to discuss and make decisions on matters affecting the community.

Committee of the Whole meetings are generally held on the first Tuesday of each month at 3:00 p.m.
From time to time, special Council meetings may be scheduled as needed.

Security Camera System Replacement
Closing Date and Time
August 17, 2026
3:00pm EDT
Submissions are to be sent electronically to:
Stacy Moffat, Special Projects Coordinator
spc@terracebay.ca
If submitting a physical copy, they may be mailed to:
The Corporation of the Township of Terrace Bay
Stacy Moffat
Special Projects Coordinator
1 Selkirk Avenue, P.O. Box 40
Terrace Bay, ON
P0T 2W0
Project Information
1. Purpose
The Corporation of the Township of Terrace Bay is seeking quotations for the supply and installation of
a new security camera system to replace its existing dated system.
The Township is seeking a reliable, modern and expandable security camera system that includes all
equipment, software, installation and support required for operation, together with as many priority
cameras as can reasonably be provided within the available project budget. The system must also
allow additional cameras or locations to be added in the future.
2. Project Objectives
The Township’s objectives for this project are to:
• Replace the Township’s dated camera system with a modern digital system;
• Provide a complete and operational system, including all required equipment, software, licensing,
installation and support;
• Replace as many of the Township’s priority existing cameras as reasonably possible within the
available project budget;
• Provide secure and user-friendly access to live and recorded footage;
• Identify any internet, networking and ongoing service requirements associated with the proposed
system; and
• Establish a system that can accommodate additional cameras and municipal locations in the future.
3. Project Locations and Priorities
The current project includes existing cameras at the following municipal locations:
• Terrace Bay Community Centre;
• Terrace Bay Swimming Pool; and
• Simcoe Plaza, where two existing cameras are located.
Priority will be given to replacing the existing cameras at these locations, together with the equipment,
software and infrastructure required to provide a complete and operational system.
One existing outdoor camera operates separately from the system being replaced and can already be
accessed remotely. Replacement or integration of this camera is considered a lower priority and may
be proposed if the available project budget permits.
The final number of cameras replaced will be determined based on the proposed system requirements,
site conditions and available project budget. Proponents may recommend alternative camera
placements where they would provide more effective coverage.
Future expansion to the Cultural Centre, Tourist Information Centre, Lighthouse or other municipal
locations is addressed in Section 5.
4. Scope of Work
The successful proponent will complete the following work:
• Review the existing camera locations, equipment and site conditions at the Terrace Bay Community
Centre, Terrace Bay Swimming Pool and Simcoe Plaza;
• Recommend an appropriate system design and camera placement;
• Supply and install a complete digital security camera system, including cameras, recording and
storage equipment, software, licensing, cabling, mounts, power supplies and all other required
components;
• Replace or remove existing equipment where required for the new installation;
• Identify any internet connection, networking, subscription, licensing or other ongoing service
requirements and associated costs;
• Configure and test the completed system;
• Provide authorized Township staff with secure access to live and recorded footage;
• Provide system documentation, warranty information and staff training;
• Include as many priority camera replacements as reasonably possible within the available budget
while ensuring the base quotation provides a complete and operational system; and
• Provide a prioritized expansion plan with separately itemized pricing for any priority camera
replacements that cannot be included in the base quotation.
The proposed system must be capable of accommodating additional cameras and municipal locations
without requiring premature replacement of the central recording, storage or management equipment.
5. Optional and Future Services
Proponents may provide separate pricing or planning information for the following:
• Replacement or integration of the newer independently operated outdoor camera;
• Future security camera coverage at the Terrace Bay Cultural Centre, Tourist Information Centre,
Terrace Bay Lighthouse or other municipal locations;
• Public-facing HD livestream coverage at Terrace Bay Beach or the Terrace Bay Lighthouse;
• Livestream capability at the arena for tournaments and events; and
• Livestream capability at the curling club for bonspiels and events.
These items must be identified and priced separately and must not reduce the equipment, installation
or priority camera replacements included in the base quotation. This information is requested for future
planning purposes and may not form part of the work awarded under this RFQ.
6. Site Reference Information
The Township has prepared a Google Earth reference map identifying the existing security camera
locations and providing supplementary site photographs.
For security reasons, access to the map will be provided to proponents upon request. Proponents may
request access by contacting:
Stacy Moffat, Special Projects Coordinator
spc@terracebay.ca
The Terrace Bay Community Centre currently has the following Tbaytel internet services:
• Fibre 1 Gbps service for the Township’s secure office network; and
• 75 Mbps service for free community Wi-Fi.
Proponents must identify whether the proposed system can use either existing connection or requires a
separate dedicated internet service.
The information in this section is provided for reference purposes only. Proponents are responsible for
verifying camera locations, existing infrastructure, site conditions and access requirements.
7. Deliverables
The successful proponent will provide:
• A fully installed and operational digital security camera system, including all required cameras,
recording and storage equipment, software, licensing, materials and other components;
• Configuration and testing of all installed components;
• Secure access to live and recorded footage for authorized Township staff;
• Confirmation of the system’s internet and network requirements, including whether a dedicated
internet service is required;
• System documentation, including camera locations, equipment details, operating instructions,
licensing information and warranty information;
• Training for designated Township staff; and
• A prioritized expansion plan with separately itemized pricing for any priority camera replacements or
future locations not included in the base quotation.
All deliverables must be completed no later than December 11, 2026.
8. Pricing Requirements
Proponents must provide clear, itemized pricing for the base quotation, including:
• Cameras and related equipment;
• Recording, storage and system management equipment;
• Software and licensing;
• Materials;
• Labour and installation;
• Travel and associated expenses;
• Configuration and testing;
• Training; and
• Any other costs required to provide a complete and operational system.
Proponents must also identify:
• Any internet, networking or connectivity requirements and associated one-time or recurring costs;
• Any licensing, subscription, maintenance or other recurring costs;
• Separate pricing for any priority camera replacements not included in the base quotation;
• Separate pricing or planning information for the optional and future services identified in Section 5;
and
• Warranty coverage and the cost of any optional extended warranty or support services.
The Township has an available 2026 project budget of $15,000, excluding HST, and is seeking a
complete and operational system within or as close as reasonably possible to this amount.
All pricing shall be provided in Canadian dollars.
9. Submission Requirements
Proponents shall provide:
• Relevant experience and qualifications;
• Proposed system design and approach;
• The number, type and proposed location of cameras included in the base quotation;
• Details regarding recording, storage, system access and future expansion capacity;
• Proposed project timeline;
• Warranty and post-installation support information;
• A prioritized expansion plan for cameras or locations not included in the base quotation;
• References for at least two comparable projects; and
• Completed pricing information in accordance with Section 8.
10. Evaluation
Submissions will be evaluated based on:
• Relevant experience and qualifications;
• Understanding of the project scope;
• Proposed system and approach;
• Equipment, coverage and overall value provided within the available budget;
• Capacity for future expansion; and
• Cost.
The Township is not obligated to accept the lowest-priced submission and may select the submission
that provides the best overall value.
11. General Conditions
The Township reserves the right to:
• Accept or reject any or all submissions;
• Request clarification or additional information from any proponent;
• Adjust the final combination of cameras and locations in consultation with the preferred proponent,
based on the available budget; and
• Cancel this RFQ without awarding a contract.

Project Completion By December 11, 2026

1. Introduction
1.1 Purpose
This report presents the findings of the site inspection and existing system review carried out at
Tillsonburg Regional Airport (CYTB) on 20 July 2026. The work was performed under the quotation issued
by Arc & Spark Electric on 26 June 2026 and approved by the Town of Tillsonburg.
The review was undertaken to establish the existing conditions relevant to the proposed installation of
four Precision Approach Path Indicator (PAPI) units held by the airport, and to determine whether that
installation is feasible.
The review addresses the electrical and site conditions relevant to the installation. Where those
conditions are conditioned by matters outside the electrical scope, this report identifies them.
1.2 Site Visit
The visit took place on Monday, 20 July 2026, beginning at 08:00. Site access and orientation were
provided by airport staff. The review covered the airport electrical service and panel, the airfield lighting
control equipment, the runway lighting installation, the four PAPI units held in storage, and the ground
conditions in the areas relevant to installation.
1.3 Scope of This Report
This report presents existing conditions, assesses those conditions against the requirements of the
proposed installation, and provides conclusions on feasibility. It identifies the inputs required to proceed
to detailed electrical design. Photographic documentation is provided in Appendix A.
The following were carried out as part of this review:
• Inspection of the electrical service, meter, main breaker and distribution panel
• Review of the existing airfield lighting power and control system, including circuit configuration,
control method, and measurement of existing circuit loading
• Assessment of the capacity of the existing circuits to accommodate the additional PAPI load
• Identification of candidate power sources, connection paths and routing constraints
• Inspection of the four PAPI units
• Visual assessment of ground and surface conditions
1.4 Obstacle Clearance
Obstacle assessment was not included in the quoted scope of this review and has not been charged for.
It is included because the electrical review was undertaken to establish whether a PAPI installation can
proceed, and whether a system can be sited at a given runway end is governed first by obstacle clearance.

Tillsonburg Regional Airport is a registered aerodrome. This report applies Transport Canada TP312, 5th
Edition, as the technical basis for assessing the proposed installation and the observations recorded on

TP312 is applied because it is the recognized Canadian standard for the design of the systems concerned,
and because the geometric and configuration requirements it sets out are the basis on which the
equipment functions as intended. Where this report identifies a departure from TP312, it states the
technical position against the standard applied. It is not a statement regarding the aerodrome's regulatory
obligations.

2. Summary of Findings
Obstacle clearance
The trees on the Runway 26 approach, approximately 635 m from the threshold, reach approximately 299
m elevation against a threshold elevation of approximately 271 m. The Obstacle Protection Surface
required for a PAPI or an APAPI at the Runway 26 end is penetrated by roughly 8 to 9 m.
The same trees sit close to the 5 percent non-instrument approach surface for Runway 26 defined in
TP312 Table 4-1(a) for Aircraft Group Number I. Screening indicates a clearance of roughly 1 to 2 m. The
elevation data was acquired in 2025, and the stand continues to grow. The Canada Flight Supplement
carries a published caution for trees east of Runway 26.
Screening of the Runway 08 approach shows no comparable obstacle.
These findings are based on the Ontario lidar-derived Digital Surface Model, which is a screening dataset
and not a survey.
Electrical service
The airport is supplied at 120/240 V, single-phase, three-wire, through a 200 A main breaker. Peak service
demand can only be established from the utility's metering records, as it varies seasonally and with airport
activity. The distribution panel has no free breaker positions.
Airfield lighting system
The airfield lighting is a parallel 120 VAC system. There is no constant current regulator and no series
circuit.
Four branch circuits serve the runway lighting. Measured currents at maximum brightness are 7.07 A, 5.31
A, 2.10 A and 2.94 A, against breaker ratings of 20 A, 15 A, 15 A and 15 A, respectively. All four circuits are

The circuits provide two brightness steps. High intensity is 120 VAC, triggered by ARCAL. Low intensity is
a reduced voltage of approximately 51 VAC obtained through variable autotransformers, triggered by a
photocell. The lights are otherwise off.

The adjournment will not affect the validity of the meeting or decisions made prior to the livestreaming being unavailable.

Please visit: https://zoom.us/ and either sign-up for a free Zoom account or continue as a guest.

DATE: Wednesday, August 26, 2026 WARD(S): 2
TITLE: PROPOSED DEMOLITION OF THE CONTRIBUTING PROPERTY
AT 8204 KIPLING AVE. WITHIN THE WOODBRIDGE HERITAGE
CONSERVATION DISTRICT
FROM:
Vince Musacchio, Deputy City Manager, Planning and Infrastructure Development
ACTION: DECISION
Purpose
Seeking an evaluation and recommendation of staff-preferred Option A, from the
Heritage Vaughan Committee for Council approval, for the relocation and conservation
of the Moody-Darker House as previously approved by Council on Feb. 22, 2023, in
response to the received application for the proposed demolition of the existing 1 ½-
storey residential structure at 8204 Kipling Ave. The subject property is designated
under Part V of the Ontario Heritage Act in the Woodbridge Heritage Conservation
District, as shown on Attachment 1. This heritage application is concurrent to the
ongoing Ontario Land Tribunal appeals filed by LCT Investment Group Ltd. for the lands
at 8158, 8196 and 8204 Kipling Ave., Tribunal file no. OLT-21-001869.
Item 1
Page 1 of 10
Page 3
Report Highlights
 The property is Designated Part V under the Ontario Heritage Act and is
identified as a contributing property in the Woodbridge Heritage Conservation
District.
 Staff does not endorse the demolition of heritage property and recommend
that the structure be relocated and conserved per the previously Council-
approved proposal on Feb. 22, 2023.
 Staff have outlined three options with varying conservation strategies and
mitigation of impacts in the ‘Analysis and Options’ section of this report, which
are not included in the Cultural Heritage Impact Assessment Addendum found
at Attachment 3. Option A for the relocation and conservation of the Moody-
Darker House is staff’s preferred option, while Option C for the
documentation, salvage, and commemoration, and ultimately the demolition
of the heritage resource, is the least preferred.
 The proposed new development on the remaining lands will be subject to a
future Heritage Vaughan review and Council Approval under section 42 of the
Ontario Heritage Act.
Recommendations
1. That Heritage Vaughan evaluates the merits of the following Options: A)
relocation and conservation; B) selective relocation and rehabilitation; or C)
documentation, salvage and commemoration (full demolition), for their
recommendation to Council for approval under Section 42 of the Ontario Heritage
Act.
2. That pursuant to Section 42 of the Ontario Heritage Act, Heritage Vaughan
recommends approval be subject to the following conditions:
a. That prior to issuance of the heritage permit for demolition (including
relocation), the owner shall enter into a Heritage Easement Agreement
pursuant to section 37 of the Ontario Heritage Act, to the satisfaction of the
City, which shall be registered on title to the lands at 8158, 8196 and 8204
Kipling Ave. at the owner’s sole cost and expense, to:
i. secure Council’s approved option and
ii. provide timeline and security for the above.
b. That the Deputy City Manager, Planning and Infrastructure Development be
the delegated authority to negotiate and execute a Heritage Easement
Agreement on behalf of the City.

Background
The subject property is a triangular-shaped parcel located between Kipling Avenue to
the east and the Canadian Pacific Railway Company lands to the west, which intersect
to the south of the property. The subject property includes an amalgamation of three
properties: 8158, 8196, and 8204 Kipling Ave. The site currently consists of open grass
fields (8158 and 8196 Kipling Ave.) and a vacant 1 ½-storey vernacular Gothic Revival
structure built circa 1880 (8204 Kipling Ave.), known as the “Moody-Darker House.”
The latter is situated on the northeast limit of the property, fronting the Meeting House
Road and Kipling Avenue intersection. The property is designated under Part V of the
Ontario Heritage Act and is a contributing property in the Woodbridge Heritage
Conservation District, within the Kipling Avenue North character area.
During its meeting on Feb. 22, 2023, Council adopted without amendment the
recommendations in Item 13, Report No. 9, of the Committee of the Whole for the
relocation, renovation, and new construction at 8204 Kipling Ave. Within that 2023
application, the Moody-Darker House was proposed to be relocated to the south of the
amalgamated property site within a park space, to accommodate the construction of 3-
storey townhouses fronting Kipling Avenue and a 5-storey midrise building fronting the
railway. A Cultural Heritage Impact Assessment was prepared by Parslow Heritage
Consultancy Inc., dated April 2021, in support of this application, Attachment 2.
In response to the requested review of the proposed plans and building design of the
current application from LCT Investment Group Ltd. for 8158, 8196 and 8204 Kipling
Ave., cultural heritage staff provided comments dated Dec. 19, 2025, stating that, per
Section 6.2.4 of the Woodbridge Heritage Conservation District Plan, “Buildings and
structures located within properties that are listed as contributing to the Woodbridge
Heritage Conservation District Heritage Character shall not be demolished and shall
remain in-situ within their existing context. The house located at 8204 Kipling Ave. is a
contributing property to the Woodbridge Heritage Conservation District.”
In June 2026, cultural heritage staff received a heritage demolition application from
Goldberg Group, on behalf of the owner, and advised the applicant that a Heritage
Review would be required for a complete application under the Ontario Heritage Act. A
Cultural Heritage Impact Assessment Addendum was subsequently prepared by
Peninsula Heritage Ltd., dated June 16th, 2026, as shown on Attachment 3.
Staff issued the Notice of Receipt on July 8, 2026, and under Ontario Heritage Act
section 42, Council has to make a decision on the application within 90 days of the
issuance of the Notice of Receipt, which will be October 6, 2026.

Vaughan Official Plan 2010
Section 6.3.2.5 of Vaughan Official Plan states “That a demolition permit for a building
or part of a building within a Heritage Conservation District shall not be issued until
plans for a replacement structure have been submitted to the City and Council has
approved the replacement structure and any related proposed landscaping features in
accordance with the relevant Heritage Conservation District Plan, the Vaughan Heritage
Conservation Guidelines and the policies of this Plan”
Considering that the planning application has been appealed to Ontario Land Tribunal,
Council is no longer the approval authority for the planning application. Staff therefore
have decided to separate the demolition application from the new construction
application under the Ontario Heritage Act and currently only request Heritage
Vaughan’s recommendation to Council regarding the status of the contributing building
located at 8204 Kipling Ave.
The new construction application on the remaining lands at 8158 and 8196 Kipling Ave.
will be brought forward for Heritage Vaughan review and Council approval at a future
date.

Analysis and Options
The applicant has proposed the demolition of the existing 1 ½-storey heritage building
built circa 1880, the Moody-Darker House.
Staff note that the current proposal’s default strategy for the demolition of the heritage
property, as outlined in the Cultural Heritage Impact Assessment Addendum,
Attachment 3, does not sufficiently review the feasibility of other mitigative measures
with the exception of documentation and salvage strategies. As a result, staff outline
three options for conservation strategies below, for purposes of Heritage Vaughan’s
evaluation and recommendation for Council approval:
Option A – relocation and conservation (staff’s preferred option)
This option is preferred and recommended by staff as it is consistent with the heritage
application previously approved by Council on Feb. 22, 2023, complies with the
Item 1

Page 6
Woodbridge Heritage Conservation District Plan, and is in keeping with good
conservation practices.
As the current site plan also includes a dedicated open space at the southernmost
portion of the subject site, similar in size as the prior heritage application’s Site Plan,
staff can endorse the relocation of the Moody-Darker House to the open space similar
to the previously approved heritage application by Council or within the development.
The relocation and conservation strategy should be outlined in a forthcoming
Conservation Plan.
Option B – selective relocation and rehabilitation
This option is considered a thoughtful compromise between staff’s preferred relocation
strategy (Option A) and the current proposal’s demolition (Option C). Staff could
endorse the selective relocation of the Moody-Darker House’s notable exterior
elevations’ heritage attributes and their rehabilitation as a commemorative feature within
the currently proposed open space’s landscape design at the southernmost portion of
the subject property. This option would enable the partial conservation of the Moody-
Darker House for valuable interpretation of the property’s history, while enabling the
new development and maintaining the heritage resource’s unique ‘sense of place’ as
well as cultural heritage value for its future residents.
The above-noted option has not been provided as an alternative to demolition by the
heritage consultant in the Cultural Heritage Impact Assessment Addendum. The scope
of documentation, salvage, and conservation strategy should be outlined in a
forthcoming Conservation Plan.
Option C – documentation, salvage and commemoration (demolition)
Staff do not endorse this option, as it is currently presented within the Cultural Heritage
Impact Assessment Addendum, shown on Attachment 3. Should this option be
Council’s preferred option, staff recommend that the existing heritage resource be
documented, its materials found to be in good condition salvaged, and the property
commemorated with salvaged materials and a plaque. The scope of documentation,
salvage, and commemoration should be outlined in forthcoming Documentation and
Commemoration Plans.
Woodbridge Heritage Conservation District Plan, 2009
The Woodbridge Heritage Conservation District Plan provides objectives, guidelines
and intervention notes for all repairs, alterations, additions and new development of
contributing properties. All proposed works within the boundary of the district must

adhere to the Plan. The following is an analysis of the objectives and guidelines which
apply to the subject property:
5.1 Objectives
1. Identify, document, maintain and restore the unique village character of
Woodbridge.
2. Conserve contributing buildings, landscapes, monuments and streetscapes.
3. Ensure new designs contribute to the Woodbridge heritage character.
4. Manage any development or redevelopment proposed within the district, in a
manner that is sensitive and responsive to all aspects necessary to ensure the
protection and conservation of the heritage resources, in order to maintain the
village character of the Woodbridge District.
5. Ensure individual heritage structures and landscapes are maintained, and new
development or redevelopment sensitively integrated, as part of a
comprehensive district.
6. Maintain Woodbridge as both a local neighbourhood and a destination for
residents of Vaughan and beyond.
7. Support a welcoming, interesting pedestrian environment by encouraging
pedestrian amenities and by maintaining human-scales development and
connections to adjacent neighbourhoods.
8. Involve area residents, property and business owners, and interested
individuals in the ongoing evolution of the Heritage Conservation District.
Section 6.2.4 Demolition of Contributing Buildings
Buildings and structures located within properties that are listed as contributing to
the Woodbridge [Heritage Conservation District] Heritage Character shall not be
demolished and shall remain in-situ within their existing context.
The contributing property at 8204 Kipling Ave., the Moody-Darker House, is currently
proposed to be demolished. Staff cannot endorse the demolition of the heritage
property, as this strategy does not comply with the Woodbridge Heritage Conservation
District Plan’s objectives. As a result, staff recommend pursuing the conservation and
commemoration strategies outlined in Options A or B above, with the relocation strategy
outlined in Option A being the preferred option.

attributes.

2. APPLICATION
2.1 Unless a separate by-law has been passed setting out a specific procedure to
be followed for a Committee, in all proceedings of Council and its Committees,
the following rules and regulations shall apply and be observed and shall be the
rules and regulations for the order and dispatch of the business in Council and
the Committees thereof:
(a) Parliamentary Authority
All matters, Points of Order or questions of procedure arising and not
provided for in the rules contained herein shall be in accordance with
“Meetings Procedures, Parliamentary Law and Rules of Order for the 21st
Century” by James Lochrie.
(b) Distribution of this By-law
Following a regular or new municipal election, the Clerk shall provide each
Member with a copy of this by-law, including amendments thereto.
(c) Amendments to this By-law
No amendment, alteration or addition to this by-law shall be made unless
due notice has been given setting forth the proposed amendment,

alteration or addition at a previous Meeting and a majority of all Members
present vote thereon.
(d) Food and Beverages at Meeting
Consumption of beverages, other than water, and the consumption of food
shall not be permitted in the Council Chambers during a Meeting.
(e) Electronic Devices
All cell phones, pagers, radios, etc. shall be switched off, non-audible or
muted during a Meeting with the exception of pagers and similar devices
carried by members of the fire service or other first responders, in the
interest of public safety.
3. CONFLICT OF INTEREST
3.1 Members are required to comply with the provisions of the Municipal Conflict of
Interest Act, R.S.O. 1990, c.M.50, as amended.
3.2 Disclosures of Interest
3.2.1 Where a Member, either on his or her own behalf or while acting for, by, with or
through another, has any Pecuniary Interest, direct or indirect, in any matter and
is present at a Meeting of the Council or local board at which the matter is the
subject of consideration, the Member:
a) Shall understand and comply with their legal obligations under the
prevailing conflict of interest legislation;
b) Shall, prior to any consideration of the matter at the Meeting, disclose the
interest and the general nature thereof;
c) Shall not take part in the discussion of, or vote on any question in respect
of the matter; and
d) Shall not attempt in any way whether, before, during or after the Meeting
to influence the voting on any such question
3.2.2 At a Meeting in which a Member discloses an interest, or as soon as possible
afterwards, the Member shall file with the Clerk, a written statement of the
interest and its general nature on the form prescribed by this By-law (attached
as Schedule “A”)

4. NOTICE OF MEETINGS
4.1 The schedule of Regular Meetings of Council shall be posted to the Township’s
website annually upon Council approval.
4.2 Notice of a Regular Meeting and all Meetings for public information shall consist
of posting of an Agenda of the said Meeting on the Township’s website, at least
three (3) days prior to the date of the Meeting.
4.3 Notice for public information of a Special Meeting shall be posted as soon as
practical with the intent of Section 4, taking into account the overriding
provisions of Subsections 5.4 and 5.5 herein.
4.4 The Township shall give notice for specific items of public interest to be
considered at Meetings, in accordance with its Notice Policy.
4.5 Any Amendments to the Agenda shall be made available to the public as soon
as is practicable prior to the Council meetings by posting the Amendment on the
Township website.
5. GENERAL ORDER OF PROCEDURES AT COUNCIL
5.1 Location
All Meetings shall be held in the Council Chambers at the Municipal
Administration Building, 31940 Highway #3, Wainfleet, unless otherwise
established in advance by resolution of Council.
5.2 Inaugural Meeting
The Inaugural Meeting after a regular election and a by-election under Section
226 (1) of the Municipal Elections Act shall be held at 7:00 p.m. on the first
Tuesday following the date of the commencement of the term of the new
Council. The opening ceremonies for the Inaugural Meeting shall be as
determined by the Clerk.
5.3 Regular Meetings
5.4 Regular Meetings shall be held in the Council Chambers at the Municipal
Administration Building every third Tuesday at 6:30 p.m. in accordance with the
Council meeting schedule prepared by the Clerk and approved by Council
resolution, unless Council, by resolution, directs otherwise.

5.5 Special Meetings
(a) The Mayor may at any time summon a Special Meeting.
(b) The Clerk shall, upon receipt of a written petition signed by a majority of
the Members, summon a Special Meeting for the purpose and at the time
and place mentioned in the petition.
(c) The Clerk shall provide all Members and the public with a minimum of
forty-eight (48) hours’ notice of all Special Meetings.
(d) Minimum notice to all Members shall consist of a telephone message
and/or email followed by a written notice and Agenda by email.
(e) The only business to be dealt with at a Special Meeting is that which is
identified in the notice of the Meeting.
(f) The lack of receipt of a notice or an Agenda for a Special Meeting by any
Member shall not affect the validity of the Meeting or any action taken
thereat.
5.6 Emergency Meetings
(a) Notwithstanding any other provision of this by-law, an Emergency Meeting
may be summoned by the Mayor to deal with an emergency or other
extraordinary situation, as determined by the Mayor in her or his sole and
unfettered discretion.
(b) The Clerk shall notify or attempt to notify all Members and the public about
the Emergency Meeting as soon as possible and in the most expedient
manner available, including, but not limited to, posting a notice on the
Township’s website.
(c) No business except business dealing directly with the emergency or
extraordinary situation shall be transacted at the Emergency Meeting.
(d) The lack of receipt of a notice or an Agenda for an Emergency Meeting by
any Member shall not affect the validity of the meeting or any action taken
thereat.
5.7 Recording and Live Streaming
(a) Regular Meetings shall be recorded electronically and, when possible,
shall be broadcast by live stream on youtube.com. At the discretion of the
Clerk in consultation with the Mayor, Special Meetings of Council may be
recorded electronically and, when possible, broadcast by live stream on

(b) Signage shall be posted in Council Chambers to ensure that presenters

The Wasaga Beach EDTAC noted that in 2026, an independent third-party
travel experience company (i.e. Lonely Planet) identified Wasaga Beach as
being the best beach for swimming in Canada. This recognition is another
important marketing asset for the Town to consider as part of its tourism
promotion efforts. The Committee engaged in discussions about how to
capitalize on this and expand the designation to have a greater impact on the
community. As a result, our advice is to undertake prolonged efforts to reach
a point where multiple entities can recommend Wasaga Beach as offering
visitors the Best Beach Experience in Canada.

 Know Before You Go
 Quality amenities

 Seasonal features

When you arrive at the beach, be it by motor vehicle access points or
pedestrian pathways, it should be a welcoming and visually stunning first
impression. Regardless of which of the eight beaches one visits one needs to
recognize and appreciate this has been maintained to support a great
experience.
It is recommended that the Town, in partnership with Ontario Parks, establish
a minimum standard of care that is publicly available and ensures the beach
areas are:

all access points (like what has been developed on Allenwood beach)
 Ease of use mechanism (feedback app) for visitors to inform and report
incidents where standards are not being maintained or require
improvements
 Installation of impressive and interesting public art installations
celebrating the unique features and heritage of the community across
the beaches.
The Committee also recommends the Town work with Ontario Parks to
consider exploring the possibility of developing a plan to make Wasaga Beach
the first garbage-free beach/park in Ontario. Under such a plan, visitors would
be required to “take it with you”. Bags to assist with removal could be
installed at designated points.
Ideally, we want the beach to be a place where people want to be seen and
take pictures, from wedding photos to sunsets to memorable family moments
that are shared and become keepsakes.

Council is being asked to endorse the Town’s application to the Skills Development
Fund (SDF) Capital Stream - GROW Pathway and approve a resolution of support for
submission to the Province as part of the application review process. This memo
provides an overview of the funding opportunity, summarizes the Whitby Fire Training
Tower and Education Campus project submitted in 2025, and outlines why a Council
resolution is needed to demonstrate municipal support and the anticipated community,
operational, and regional benefits of the proposed project.
The Ontario Skills Development Fund (SDF) Capital Stream - GROW Pathway supports
capital projects that build, expand, renovate, or modernize training facilities to increase
workforce training capacity in high-demand sectors. Municipalities are eligible
applicants, and approved projects may receive provincial funding for up to 49% of
eligible project costs. In July 2025, the Town of Whitby applied to the 2024-2025 round
of funding for the Whitby Fire Training Tower and Education Campus. The project would
expand emergency services training capacity, support workforce development, and
strengthen local and regional emergency preparedness.
The proposed Whitby Fire Training Tower and Education Campus builds on the existing
Fire Training Tower project by adding an Education Building and complementary
training infrastructure. The expansion includes dedicated classroom and training space,
an auto-extraction training pad, training equipment storage, mobile washroom facilities,
and advanced training technology such as virtual reality simulation software, laptops,
and tablets. Together, these investments would create a comprehensive training
campus to support modern firefighter and emergency services training.
Page 6 of 43
If approved, the funding would help increase local training capacity, reduce reliance on
external training facilities, and support more predictable access to training for Whitby
Fire and Emergency Services. The expanded campus is expected to accommodate
approximately 250 trainees annually and serve as a long-term municipal asset
supporting workforce development, operational readiness, and public safety for Whitby
and the broader Durham Region.
The Town’s application seeks approximately $2.54 million in provincial funding,
representing the program’s maximum contribution of 49% of eligible project costs. The
total eligible project cost is estimated at $5.19 million. The remaining $2.65 million
would be funded through the existing approved capital budget.
The SDF Capital Stream - GROW Pathway permits eligible project costs incurred after
the launch of the program in June 2023 to be considered for funding reimbursement,
subject to provincial approval and the terms of the Transfer Payment Agreement. This
provision may allow the Town to include eligible project planning, design, and other
approved capital-related expenditures already incurred as part of the Fire Training
Campus project. The Town has updated the province on the status of the current Fire
Training Tower construction.
Since submitting the application, the Town has continued to respond to the Province’s
requests for additional information. On August 11, 2026, the Town received the most
recent correspondence requesting documentation that demonstrates municipal support
and confirms the need for the proposed project. The Ministry advised that Council
resolutions of support will be considered as part of the application review process.
The Ministry has advised that Council resolutions should clearly explain how the
municipality expects to use, access, or benefit from the proposed training facility.
Resolutions that outline anticipated training, operational, or regional benefits provide
more useful context than general statements of support by demonstrating the project’s
expected outcomes and impact.
Included below is proposed recommendation and draft resolution wording for Council’s
consideration.
